protocol.name: spatiand_xr_v1

description.summary: stereoscopic and head-tracked surfaces

protocol.description:
This is a protocol about applications, not about video. Any application may want to be stereoscopic -- a modelling tool, a map, a game, a terminal with depth to it -- and the compositor's job is to let it appear the way it means to appear, whatever it draws. A media player is only the first client.
Three things a Wayland client needs in order to draw for a head, and cannot get any other way:
1. a way to say how the two eyes' views are packed into its buffer, 2. a way to say what the surface *is* in the world -- a panel, something pinned to the view, a pair of eye views, or the sky itself, 3. the head and eye poses, before it renders.
Everything else it already has. A wl_buffer is the swapchain, a frame callback is the frame loop, a wl_surface is the layer. This protocol deliberately adds nothing that Wayland already carries.
HYBRID CLIENTS
A client that binds nothing here is an ordinary window, and an ordinary window is what it stays. Every request below is opt-in and every one has a defined meaning on a compositor that is showing the surface flat. The intended shape is one application that runs on a normal desktop, runs as a flat window here, and turns itself stereoscopic or immersive when it finds this global -- not three applications, and not a mode switch.
COORDINATES
This protocol's frame is **OpenXR's**, not the compositor's: +X right, +Y up, -Z forward, right-handed, metres, and quaternions in (x, y, z, w) order. The compositor's own frame is different and is not exposed here.
That is a deliberate choice at the boundary. It makes an OpenXR adapter a memcpy rather than a translation layer, and it means every convention a VR developer already has in their fingers is the right one. The structures in the pose channel are field-compatible with XrPosef and XrFovf for the same reason.
UNITS ON THE WIRE
Wayland has no floating point. The rarely-sent values here are signed integers in micro-units: micrometres for distance, microradians for angle. The per-frame values are not on the wire at all -- see the pose channel.

interface.name: spatiand_xr_v1

description.summary: stereoscopic and head-tracked surfaces

interface.description: The factory. Binding it says nothing and changes nothing.

description.summary: destroy the factory

request.name: get_xr_surface

description.summary: extend a surface with stereo and layer state

request.description: One per wl_surface for its lifetime. Requesting a second is a protocol error, because two objects setting the layout of one surface have no defined resolution.

request.name: get_pose_channel

description.summary: ask for the shared-memory pose channel

request.description: See spatiand_xr_pose_channel_v1. A client that only shows pre-packed stereo -- a side-by-side film, say -- does not need this and should not ask for it: it is the compositor's head tracking, and asking for it while not using it is the difference between a player and a headset application.

entry.name: surface_exists
entry.summary: the surface already has an xr object

entry.name: bad_layer
entry.summary: layer value not in the enum

entry.name: bad_layout
entry.summary: eye layout value not in the enum

interface.name: spatiand_xr_surface_v1

description.summary: how a surface is drawn for two eyes

interface.description: All state here is double-buffered: it takes effect on the next wl_surface.commit, like everything else about a surface. Changing layout between frames is expected and costs nothing -- a player showing a side-by-side film with a flat menu over it changes it twice a second.

request.name: destroy

description.summary: stop treating this surface specially

request.description: The surface reverts to mono, layer "window", on the next commit.

request.name: set_eye_layout

description.summary: how the two eyes are packed into the buffer

request.description:
With "mono" both eyes are shown the same pixels; this is the default and is what a surface that never calls this does.
For the split layouts the two eyes sample opposite halves of the SAME buffer while the surface keeps ONE position in the world. Full-width and half-width side-by-side are not distinguished, because they are not different: each eye is given its half stretched across the surface, and only the sharpness differs. Send the source as it is.

entry.name: mono
entry.summary: both eyes see the whole buffer

entry.name: side_by_side
entry.summary: left eye in the left half

entry.name: top_bottom
entry.summary: left eye in the top half

request.name: set_eye_swapped

description.summary: the halves are the other way round

request.description: Some sources are packed right-eye-first and nothing in the file says so. A viewer needs a control for that which does not mean re-encoding.

request.name: set_layer

description.summary: what this surface is in the world

request.description: See the layer enum. A compositor that cannot honour a layer -- the sky is already taken, say -- answers with layer_refused and keeps drawing the surface as a window, which is always a valid thing to be.

entry.name: window

description.summary: an ordinary panel in the room

entry.description: The default. Moved and resized by the wearer, stays where it is put. The OpenXR quad layer is this.

entry.name: head_locked

description.summary: a panel that follows the view

entry.description: Keeps its angular size and position relative to the head. For content that must stay in front of you, and for a client doing its own head tracking -- a nested runtime, say -- where the compositor moving the surface as well would apply tracking twice.

entry.name: projection

description.summary: the client has rendered the two eye views itself

entry.description: The buffer is what the eyes should see, drawn by the client from the poses in the pose channel, and is presented filling the view rather than as a panel in it. Requires an eye layout other than mono. The OpenXR projection layer is this.

entry.name: equirect_180

description.summary: the client is the sky, front hemisphere

entry.description: Equirectangular, covering 180 degrees of longitude in front of the wearer. Behind them there is no image and the compositor says so rather than smearing the edge.

description.summary: the client is the sky, all of it

request.name: set_yaw_offset

description.summary: turn an immersive image about the vertical axis

request.description: Microradians. Only meaningful for the equirect layers, where it brings the interesting part of a panorama round to face the wearer's forward. Ignored otherwise.

event.name: layer_refused

description.summary: the compositor will not do that

event.description: The surface keeps whatever layer it had. Carries the layer that was asked for, so a client that asked for two things knows which failed, and a human-readable reason which is for a log and not for a user.

event.name: layer_lost

description.summary: an exclusive layer has been taken away

event.description: Sent when the wearer or another client takes back something only one surface can have -- the sky. The surface is a window again from the next frame. A client that crashes cannot leave the wearer inside a frozen image, because the same thing happens when its surface dies.

interface.name: spatiand_xr_pose_channel_v1

description.summary: head and eye poses, in shared memory

interface.description:
Poses are NOT sent as events, and that is the central decision in this protocol.
A head-tracked client has to know where the head is at the last possible moment before it renders -- that is what makes the world stay still. An event carrying the pose is already stale when it arrives: it costs a round trip, it arrives when the compositor got round to sending it rather than when the client needs it, and it cannot be re-read a millisecond later without another round trip.
So the compositor writes poses into a small ring in shared memory and hands over a read-only file descriptor. The client maps it once and reads the newest sample whenever it likes, including immediately before submitting a frame. No round trips, no per-frame protocol traffic, and late-latching becomes a memory read.
The ring also carries a short history, so a client can interpolate to an arbitrary time -- which is exactly what an OpenXR adapter needs to answer xrLocateViews for a predicted display time.
MEMORY FORMAT
Little-endian, naturally aligned, and stable for the life of this interface version. All floats are IEEE-754 binary32. Times are CLOCK_MONOTONIC nanoseconds, the same clock a frame callback's time comes from.
struct spatiand_xr_channel { // offset 0 uint32_t version; // 1 uint32_t slot_count; // power of two uint32_t slot_stride; // bytes uint32_t slots_offset; // bytes from the start uint64_t write_index; // total slots ever written uint64_t _reserved; };
struct spatiand_xr_slot { // slots_offset + (i * slot_stride) uint64_t seq; // odd while being written int64_t sample_ns; // when this pose was measured int64_t predicted_ns; // when a frame submitted now is expected to be shown int64_t _reserved; float head_orientation[4]; // x, y, z, w -- XrQuaternionf float head_position[3]; // metres -- XrVector3f float _pad0; struct { float orientation[4]; // x, y, z, w float position[3]; // metres, relative to the tracking origin float _pad; float fov[4]; // angleLeft, angleRight, angleUp, angleDown // radians, signed -- XrFovf exactly } eye[2]; // 0 = left };
READING IT
Read `write_index`, take slot `(write_index - 1) modulo slot_count` (the count is a power of two, so this is a mask), read `seq`, read the body, read `seq` again. If either `seq` read is odd or the two differ, the writer was in that slot: step back one slot or try again. This is an ordinary seqlock and it never blocks the compositor.
The compositor writes at its own rate, which is the display rate. A client that reads faster will see repeats; one that reads slower will miss samples. Neither is an error.

request.name: destroy

description.summary: stop receiving poses

request.description: The mapping stays valid until the client unmaps it, but stops being updated.

event.name: channel

description.summary: here is the shared memory

event.description: Sent once, immediately. The descriptor is read-only and sealed; map it with MAP_SHARED and PROT_READ.

event.name: unavailable

description.summary: there are no poses to give

event.description: Sent instead of `channel` when the session has no head tracking at all -- no headset plugged in, or a nested session on a desktop. A client should carry on as a flat window rather than wait. It is not an error and the object stays alive; `channel` may arrive later if a headset appears.
